tn.quote: Chatino tone is a feature of the word, and is contrastive only on the final syllable. Unstressed syllables carry a non-contrastive tone which may be identical with the final tone of the utterance preceding it in a stream of speech. We posit the following phonemic tones: [table] upglide 21 32 43 / level 2 3 4 / downglide 12 23. These tones may be elicited after pause or after a tone /3/ in nouns and adjectives. Tone plays a heavy role in Chatino syntax, but after a preliminary study of the complex verb system no additional contrastive tones have been encountered.

4397.dq: No description of stress exists; the only mention is the carried metrical premise 'a series of six trochaic tetrameters catalectic based on word-initial stress with syllabic quantities ignored' (Poultney 1979 as quoted by Di Carlo 2006: 29), whose premise names word-initial stress but describes no prosodic domain.
4397.heavy: not applicable; Poultney's premise explicitly disregards quantity ('with syllabic quantities ignored')
4397.prule: None stated. The only linguistic monograph on the language (Di Carlo 2006) has no accent/stress statement in its phonology chapter (ch. 2 'Analisi fonologica', pp. 13-25); at p. 29, in the section on word boundaries, it reports without endorsing it Poultney 1979's metrical conjecture that the long Novilara inscription (PID 343) scans as six catalectic trochaic tetrameters 'based on word-initial stress with syllabic quantities ignored', and uses that scansion only as corroboration for word division. Word-initial stress is therefore a metrical premise applied to an untranslated ~60-word text, not an observed or described stress rule.

Secondary stress in non-compound words is not described.

4399.dloc: Köhncke 2011 p. 271, last page of ch. 2.4.2 'Die Konsonanten', with fn. 1500 (Warnkross 1912: 10); continuation p. 272.
4399.prule: Main stress on the lexical stem syllable (Stammsilbe): prefixes are unstressed and reduce (vesábm), derivational/inflectional syllables are weak; in compounds the first stem syllable carries the main stress (Warnkross 1912: 10 via fn. 1500). Loans and a few compounds are stressed on a non-initial syllable (Meschíen 'Maschine', Mesík 'Musik', Tebáck, Motór, Bürgeméister on the head noun, Améisn). Position follows morphological structure (stem vs affix), not syllable count or weight.
4399.srule: Only for compounds: the first stem syllable carries the strong stress; the second stem syllable also carries it only while the word is still felt as a compound (Warnkross 1912: 10, Wolgast, quoted in Köhncke 2011: 271 fn. 1500). Secondary or rhythmic stress in non-compound words is not mentioned in Köhncke 2011, pp. 271-272 (one loan transcribed „ámesìern“ 'amüsieren' with a grave, without comment).

4400.heavy: Heavy = (C)VC with a lax vowel (word-internal closed syllable, bimoraic); light = (C)V open syllable, including phonetically long/tense vowels and diphthongs ('CV syllables generally count as light. This means that the respective phonetically long vowels are monomoraic', p. 154); superheavy = final CVVC (phonetically overlong tense vowel) or CVCC, whose final C is extrasyllabic, leaving a heavy CVV<C>/CVC<C>; a plain final CVC in polysyllables does not attract stress ('their weight in word-final position basically depends on the segmental context', p. 154); schwa syllables never stressed.
4400.dflt: Antepenult: 'trochaic stress is assigned generally to the rightmost non-final heavy syllable or else to the rightmost non-final sequence of two light syllables' (p. 122); in bisyllables 'As soon as two light syllables... are available, stress surfaces word-initially. The respective foot structure is then (LL)' (p. 145).
4400.prule: Primary word stress falls within the last three syllables of the prosodic word, assigned by moraic trochees from the right: on the penult if it is (C)VC (closed, lax vowel, heavy); if the penult is (C)V (open, light, even with a phonetically long tense vowel or diphthong) stress moves to the antepenult, whether that is (C)VC or (C)V; a superheavy final syllable (CVVC with overlong vowel / CVCC, final C extrasyllabic) takes final stress; schwa syllables are never stressed. CV.CVC bisyllables regularly take penult stress (Table 24 a: tobak, kivt, dorüm); the CV.CVC bisyllables with final stress (Table 24 b: kajüt, kapell, kapun) and loans like sombrero, bikini are Romance loanwords analysed as carrying lexically pre-specified stress (ID-STR) outside the weight rule.
4400.srule: Exists but placement not analysed: Prehn treats secondary stress 'only where necessary' (p. 121) and ignores 'possible secondary stress' in the tableaux (p. 140); the one remark (fn. 127, p. 125) is that 'Alkoven' [ alko n] 'alcove' (CVC.CV.CəC, primary on the antepenult) has secondary stress on the penult rather than the schwa ultima. 4402.prule: Primary (strong) stress on the final syllable of the word, whatever its length or syllable type: monosyllables in isolation are stressed; native disyllables (presyllable + main syllable) and disyllabic compounds stress the ultima; polysyllables stress the ultima. Fixed-final, quantity-insensitive.
4402.srule: Secondary (moderate, grave-marked) stress on the first syllable of polysyllables (three or more syllables; the examples are loans), primary on the ultima: /tòorəsáp/ 'telephone', /wìtsəwɔkɔ́ɔn/ 'engineer'. Disyllables (native presyllable + main syllable, and disyllabic compounds) carry the final primary only; their first syllable is unmarked (tertiary/weak).
4402.quote: There are 3 degrees of stress: primary or strong, secondary or moderate, and tertiary or weak. Primary and secondary stress are represented by the acute and grave respectively while tertiary stress is unmarked. As in the standard, monosyllables uttered in isolation take primary stress: /báan/ '[I] can [do it]', /srúuəl/ '[It's] easy'; dissyllables of native provenance take primary stress on the ultima: /cənnə́ər/ 'ladder', /ləmbáak/ 'trouble'. The same pattern obtains in dissyllabic compounds: /koon kóon/ 'children', /pləəw tnɔ́l/ 'road, highway'. Polysyllables take primary stress on the ulti…

evidence_works.detail: Author is a native speaker of the Surin variety: sec. 1.4 p. 14 'I was born in Ban Koh Tlung, Tambon Burasri, Amphoe Muang, Surin. I speak Northern Khmer as my mother tongue. So I elicited the data and described the grammatical system of the language by myself, and then checked the data with my mother-in-law, Mrs. Chaey Sujinpram, a 74-year-old woman who has lived in the area since her birth'; sec. 1.6 p. 15: the village is 'located 9 kilometers east of Surin'; sec. 1.7 Methodology p. 15: 'I collected data by myself. The data are based on my knowledge of Northern Khmer as a native speaker. Additional information is from my mother-in-law as stated in Sec.1.4 p.14.' No dedicated stress section and no explicit placement rule. What it adds to the entry: (a) foot structure, 1.10.3 p. (b) 2.2.3.2 In Unstressed Syllables: 'Unstressed syllables in Northern Khmer may often be reduced and have freely varying allomorphs'; 2.4.2 Reduction p. 52: 'the unstressed presyllables of disyllabic words are the least stable, and tend to undergo change in rapid speech', with reduction patterns 1-6 for presyllables (e.g. p. 52 /kancɒp --> kəncɒp --> kcɒp/ 'to wrap, pack'), which is the presyllable = unstressed, main syllable = stressed pattern; (c) compounds, 2.4.2 item 7 p. 54: '/pram/ "five" is subject to extreme reduction when it does not carry primary stress: /pram-mɷ:j --> prəm-mɷ:j --> pmɷ:j/ "six"' (vowel as printed, closed omega; the row quote writes mɔ:j), and 2.4.3.6 p. 66: 'Compounds are phonologically close-knit and they become one foot (one stress group); but noun phrases are not', p. 67: 'In compounds, if the first element is a long vowel it is usually reduced to a short vowel' - the compound is one stress group and its non-final element is reduced, which refines the WORD domain: compound = one stress group, noun phrase = more than one. (d) The thesis's only stress-marked compound, 3.1.3.3 Semantic Prosodies p. 194, '(a) Stress:', contrasts /'kon-proh/ (Compound Noun) 'a son' with /ko:n 'proh/ (Noun phrase) 'a male child (i.e. not a female child)' and /nsɯ: 'ɲom/ 'my book (i.e. not yours, hers, etc.)': the stress mark stands before the first element of the compound but on the final element of the emphasised phrases; whether the compound mark denotes first-element stress or the single stress group of the whole compound is not stated, so this passage is filed as a point to adjudicate rather than as agreement with Jenner's ultima statement for compounds. Symbols list p. xviii (' = stress; a curved rising arrow = stress and rising pitch), 3.2.3.3.1 p. 232 ('A stress and a rising pitch is put on the element to be emphasized'), p. 194 (a)-(d) and the clause-level remarks on pp. 248 and 337 concern emphatic phrase-level prominence, not lexical placement.

4403.heavy: n/a: vowel length is phonemic in Kumandin (tar 'порох' vs ta:r 'мешок', p. 79) and the source rules quantity out as the main stress correlate (p. 81, citing Zinder); stress position is not conditioned on syllable weight.
4403.prule: Fixed final, quantity-insensitive: main word stress falls on the last syllable of the word-form; when affixes are added it moves to the new final syllable (with some unspecified exceptions). Phonetic correlate: an obligatory F0 rise / pitch peak on the final syllable in every word-form type, optionally accompanied by duration and intensity (p. 84); Baskakov 1972: 38, as reported on p. 79, had the same placement ('fixed, as a rule, on the last syllable of the word') but called it expiratory.
4403.srule: None: Seljutina 1998: 80-81 raises and then refutes a hypothesised secondary, length-based stress on the initial syllable ('...что опровергает предположение о наличии в языке кумандинцев второстепенного долготного ударения на первом слоге (или на одном из первых слогов)', p. 81); initial-syllable vowel lengthening is phonemic/positional length, not stress, and the only word stress is the final-syllable pitch peak (p. 84).
4403.quote: [p. 84] Обязательным, стабильным для всех типов словоформ является повышение ЧОТ в конце словоформы, что позволяет рассматривать финально-слоговой высотный пик как определяющий компонент кумандинского словесного ударения, факультативно сопровождающийся дополнительными компонентами длительности и интенсивности. 4403.exq_: p. 84: 'подвижное — всякий раз при наращении аффиксов перемещающееся (за некоторыми исключениями) на последний слог'; p. 79 (reporting Baskakov 1972: 38): 'фиксированное, как правило, на последнем слоге слова'. The hedge is mild ('with some exceptions', 'as a rule') and the exceptions are not named…
4403.tone: Not a tone language. Seljutina calls Kumandin word stress 'musical' (музыкальное) because its obligatory component is an F0 rise ending in a pitch peak on the final-syllable vowel (pp. 83-84: 'постепенно восходящее движение основного тона с тоновым пиком на гласном конечного слога'), with duration and intensity optional; Baskakov had called it expiratory (p. 79). This is a claim about the phonetic correlate of a fixed-position word stress, not a tonal or pitch-accent system.

4405.dq: In B “ bad ” = mehe with the final e low, and “ good ” = mehe with the final e high—an excellent example of the great importance of tone in the language.
4405.dloc: p. 290 fn. 1; context p. 285 (B = 'the language of the Northern group' of Western Rengmas, standard = upper khels of Tesophenyu) and p. 287 (spelling key, tones noted only where of special importance)
4405.prule: No word-stress or accent rule is stated. The first-hand prosodic statements for B (Northern Rengma) are that lexical tone is of 'great importance', shown by two final-syllable minimal pairs: mehe 'bad' (final e low) vs mehe 'good' (final e high) (p. 290 fn. 1; vocabulary p. 309 kemehe) and ayi 'hail' (last syllable on a high note) vs ayi 'earth' (on a low note) (p. 246 fn. 1; ayi = 'hail' in B per p. 245).
4405.quote: In B “ bad ” = mehe with the final e low, and “ good ” = mehe with the final e high—an excellent example of the great importance of tone in the language. [p. 290 fn. 1] ... No one but a specialist can ever hope adequately to analyse a Naga language, with its tones, its rich vocabulary and its nuances of meaning that are so hard to grasp. [p. 285] ... I have used no diacritical marks, and tones have only been noted where of special importance. Only syllables which are very strongly long or short have been so marked. [p. 287]

4405.tone: Mills treats all three Rengma languages as tonal ('a Naga language, with its tones', p. 285) but marks tones only 'where of special importance' (p. 287). For B (Northern Rengma) he gives two lexical tone minimal pairs, both on the final syllable: (i) ayi 'hail' (last syllable on a high note) vs ayi 'earth' (on a low note), p. 246 fn. 1 -- ayi is listed as the B word for 'hail' on p. 245 ('hail (legweng, A; ayi, B; awe, C)') and the footnoted form is that of 'the Tesophenyu group', i.e. Mills' Northern group = the language-B villages; (ii) mehe 'bad' (final e low) vs mehe 'good' (final e high), p. 290 fn. 1, repeated in the comparative vocabulary p. 309, B column: kemehe (final e high) 'good' / kemehe (final e low) 'bad'. Tone remarks for A: pronoun a 'I' (on low note) vs a 'he' (on high note), p. 295; conditional zolo 'if he says' with 'the final o... on a higher note than in the imperative termination', p. 301 fn. 1; haduki 'the day after to-morrow' (the u on a low note) vs haduki 'on the third day' (the u on a high note), p. 304. Intonation: negative questions use the ordinary negative verb, 'the tone of voice indicating the question', p. 303. A whole-book search for stress/accent/emphasis finds no statement on word stress or accent for any of the three languages; 'stress' occurs only non-linguistically (p. 50, 'one of the great stresses of the family complex').

Somé 1982], dont la réalisation est provoquée par l'abaissement d'un ton haut par un ton bas réalisé ou flottant (voir sur ce point Stewart [1983]). Il peut être actualisé à l'intérieur ou entre les constituants. Il est représenté par le symbole /'/ indiquant le changement de niveau tonal. tn.translation: 2.1 The tonal system. Dagara has a two-tone system: a high tone /´/ and a low tone /`/, plus a downstep [P.-A. 4417.prule: No stress rule: word prosody is Japanese-type lexical pitch accent, notated as pitch rise 「 and fall 」 on citation forms with and without a particle. Systems vary by village within the language: Naze town, Tatsugo Toguchi and Naze Ashikebu are multi-pattern (多型) accent systems (Naze n+1 classes, §6.3; Ashikebu a register (式) contrast, Pn=2n-1, §7.2.2); Sani (Kasari) and, per Uwano's survey, every Kasari-Tatsugo village have N-pattern contrasts (Sani a 3-pattern system α/β/γ with α ○「○(…)= taken by the overwhelming majority of 2+-mora words, γ created by fusion of the first two morae or an initial devoiced mora). For Yamato and Sumiyo villages (central Ōshima) Uwano states that no dialect has yet been confirmed as truly one-pattern (accentless) either; e.g. 'crawl' ha「juN beside the native 「hojuN (< 「ho:juN) (p. 50). Overall Uwano's summary: Amami dialects are predominantly N-pattern with multi-pattern systems scattered among them (p. 45).

4417.tone: Uwano 2000 describes only pitch accent (アクセント = pitch rise/fall patterns; the words ストレス/強弱/強さ do not occur anywhere in the paper (full-text search negative)). Northern Ōshima villages: Naze town multi-pattern n+1 system (11) p. 47; Toguchi multi-pattern (6) p. 45; Ashikebu register contrast (18) p. 50, Pn=2n-1; Sani 3-pattern (15) p. 49 with α dominant and the contrasts recent (tonogenesis from mora fusion / initial devoicing, §7); every Kasari-Tatsugo village has accent distinctions per Uwano 1996b; Yamato and Sumiyo (central Ōshima): no dialect yet confirmed as truly one-pattern (p. 50, sentence running across the column break: 確認できた | 方言はまだない). Contrary village-level report checked (Shigeno 2010, Ura (Amami Ryukyuan), §2.5 p. 18): 'Ura does not have lexically distinctive pitch. The default pitch pattern is LH for bimoraic words, LHH for trimoraic words, and so on.' with p. 17 'Ura is one of the North Ōshima dialects.' Either way the prosody is pitch, not stress, and no stress rule is stated by any reachable source.

4418.tone: Slave is a tone language with lexical (and grammatical) high tone; stress is not distinctive (Rice 1989: 46). Hare verbs show a tone shift: lexical stem high tone surfaces on the prestem vowel with low tone on the stem (Rice 1989 ch. 8; Rice 1990 sec. 3.3), while in nouns and postpositions the stem high tone stays on the stem (Rice 1990: 230). The prominence is independent of pitch: Rice 1987 fn. 5: 'I am not sure just what the phonetic correlate of what I am calling intensity is. It is definitely not pitch, as pitch as clearly discernible as tone in Hare. It appears to have to do with intensity and perhaps duration.' Rice 1987 (pp. 8-9) states the intensity difference for low-tone syllables: 'In these verbs, the prestem syllable is phonetically more intense or stronger than the stem syllable is'; in nouns and postpositions 'the vowel of the stem is of greater intensity than the vowel of the prestem syllable when both are low tone'. A prefix vowel bearing lexical high tone gains extra intensity in all dialects (Rice 1989: 46, excerpt grade).

variants.prule: Stress is not distinctive in Slave, a two-tone (high/low) language. In the Hare dialect there are predictable 'stress-like properties': what might be called stress generally falls on the vowel immediately preceding the stem of a VERB and on the STEM vowel of a NOUN; intensity is the primary phonetic correlate (details deferred to chapter 8, the tone chapter). In prefixes in all dialects, a vowel with lexical high tone on which a high tone falls has extra stress, i.e. is more intense; e.g. the 1sg and 3sg perfective differ only by tone placement, and a high tone landing on an already high-toned vowel gives it prominent stress.
variants.quote: Stress is not a distinctive feature [in] Slave. In the Hare dialect, there are stress-like properties which are predictable. What might be called stress generally falls on the vowel immediately preceding the stem of a verb and on the stem vowel of a noun. A stressed vowel is generally acoustically more intense than an unstressed vowel, and intensity is in fact the primary phonetic correlate of stress. See chapter 8. In prefixes in all dialects, a high tone may fall on a vowel with lexical high tone. That vowel then has extra stress, or is more intense. ... In the perfective, the first and third person singular forms differ only by tone placement. Where the high tone falls on a vowel already bearing a high tone, as in the first person singular perfective form, this vowel retains its tone and receives prominent stress.

4419.dq: Word stress is assigned after CG applies, with no consideration of whether a given syllable has or has not been altered by CG. Whereas CG affects alternate syllables, as explained below, resembling Yupik prosody in this respect, word stress is assigned individually to syllables practically regardless of what precedes or follows.
4419.heavy: 'the non-final closed syllables and all long vowels—including diphthongs and vowel clusters, which are phonetically long—receive stress'; 'A long consonant, like a consonant cluster, has the effect of closing the preceding syllable'. So heavy = CVV/diphthong/vowel cluster anywhere, and CVC (cluster- or geminate-closed) only when non-final; a word-final closed syllable is not heavy by closure alone.
4419.dflt: None: a word of light syllables only is 'equally stressless' (iřítuq gets its stress only because CG lengthens t and closes the second syllable); no fallback position is stated.
4419.prule: Quantity-driven, non-culminative word stress: every heavy syllable is stressed, where heavy = any non-final closed syllable (closed by a consonant cluster or a long/geminate consonant, underlying or created by Consonant Gradation) and any syllable with a phonetically long nucleus (long vowel aa/ii/uu, diphthong ai/au, or vowel cluster iu/ui/ia/ua) in any position; light (short open) syllables are unstressed, and a word whose syllables are all light is 'equally stressless'. Long vowels and diphthongs are stressed over their whole quantity; vowel clusters carry stress on their second member except word-finally (úi, niγiřúaq). Stress is assigned syllable by syllable after Consonant Gradation, with no fixed edge, no rhythm and no designated primary peak.
4419.srule: Not mentioned in Kaplan 1985 (section 2, pp. 193-194; whole article pp. 191-210): the stresses of a word are not ranked; every heavy syllable is stressed equally (Inúktuyúuq) and an all-light word is 'equally stressless'.

4422.srule: Not mentioned in Brockway, Brockway & Santos Valdés 2018, Gramática náhuatl §1 Fonología y ortografía (pp. 325-328; §1.4 Acento, p. 328), nor in Brockway 1979: 145; neither source speaks of secondary or rhythmic stress or says a word has only one stress.
